geral.texto: Clair responds directly to conversation addressed to her (small talk): she greets the group (the greeting 'Hi everyone, my name is Clair…'; the author reports that she also greets when two people join the chat [to be confirmed: how the server decides this]), confirms she is still there, says how she is doing and who she is. When people ask for help, she suggests asking their partner, and when they ask a content question, she says she does not know enough to answer. Her role is to facilitate discussion among people, not to be a source of answers. These responses exist in all modes read (in each language of the mode). What changes from one mode to another is the set of moves (talk moves), the conversation signals that decide when to intervene, and the available languages.

modos.em_uma_frase: The reference repertoire of Academically Productive Talk: eight moves to deepen reasoning and get participants to listen to each other.
modos.o_nome: APT stands for Academically Productive Talk, the talk moves framework Clair builds on. 'Base' marks the core set of moves from that tradition, with no explicit pedagogical goals and no content from a specific topic. That is why it is the default: it works with any subject and serves as a baseline for comparing the other modes.
modos.o_conjunto: The eight moves serve three functions. Deepening what someone said (extend the reasoning, ask for an example). Getting peers to listen to each other (agree or disagree, restate in their own words, add on, link their own idea to another's, build on what has been said). And organizing what the group has built so far (recap). Several moves address a person by name and speak of the 'partner': they hand the floor back to the participants instead of answering for them, which fits a Clair that does not teach content.
modos.como_age: Each move has a rule that combines dialogue state signals (dominance and coordination, type of utterance such as initiating or arguing, similarity to the topic, time and pace). It only acts when certainty exceeds 0.75. For example, the recap is tied to low similarity to the topic and high time, and 'agree or disagree' to argumentation with high coordination. [to be confirmed]

cuidados: No move is tied to silence: someone who stays quiet goes unnoticed (compare with apt-goals). [to be confirmed]

modos.em_uma_frase: APT organized by pedagogical goals: Clair can start the conversation on her own, invite those who are quiet, redirect back to the lesson and propose hypothetical questions.
modos.o_nome: 'Goals' indicates that the moves are no longer a flat repertoire and now serve numbered goals: check-in is goal 1; redirecting, coordinating peers and getting them to ask each other questions are goal 2; what-if is goal 3; pressing for reasoning is goal 4. The numbering suggests a progression, from keeping people participating and on task to requiring justification [to be confirmed].
modos.o_conjunto: Six moves, and this changes Clair's role: instead of only reacting to what was said, she also looks after those who are not speaking. The check-in invites the group to share their progress; the redirect brings the discussion back to the lesson; coordination asks one peer to help another with the next step; peer questions encourage asking a peer rather than her; the what-if poses a hypothesis ('what would happen if…'); and pressing for reasoning asks for elaboration or an example. Three of the moves have ready-made follow-up questions (for example, asking the author to explain why they think so), so Clair leads short sequences, not isolated comments.
modos.como_age: According to the rules, the check-in depends on the TSLM signal and on time, the redirect on the COFF signal, peer coordination on coordination between peers with no question and on the L3_CU signal, and peer questions on the TSLQ signal [to be confirmed: the meaning of TSLM, COFF and TSLQ; I read them as time since last message, conversation off topic and time since last question]. Since she can speak without a triggering message, the interface needs to poll the server periodically (proactive check).

modos.em_uma_frase: Motivational support instead of pressure for reasoning: three moves that offer choice and reinforce competence and connection among peers.
modos.o_nome: This is Self-Determination Theory, which identifies three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. The mode's three moves carry exactly these names, so the design translates the theory directly: instead of demanding more argumentation, Clair tries to sustain the motivation to keep talking.
modos.o_conjunto: Autonomy: invites the person to elaborate or give an example, but makes it explicit that they may prefer to continue the conversation ('I appreciate your choice'). Competence: links the utterance to what has already been discussed and then reinforces that each contribution improves understanding. Relatedness: asks how the ideas match or differ from the peer's and thanks them for sharing. The repertoire is minimal: one sentence per move, plus two thank-you messages per move. This is a mode for observing the effect of a supportive tone, not for variety of interventions.
modos.como_age: Decides with few signals (type of utterance, closeness to the topic, pace) and stays quiet when the message is a question. [to be confirmed]

modos.em_uma_frase: Socially shared regulation of learning: interventions aimed at the whole group, about understanding, joint planning, participation and climate.
modos.o_nome: SSRL usually stands for Socially Shared Regulation of Learning, the regulation of learning that the group carries out together [to be confirmed]. The five moves say the same: cognitive, metacognitive, behavioral, socioemotional and shared perspective. The focus shifts from individual contribution to how the group functions.
modos.o_conjunto: The sentences address everyone ('explain to each other', 'how could you help each other'), without calling anyone by name, unlike APT. Each move has 3 or 4 variations, the most varied repertoire among the modes. Cognitive: deals with confusion and shared understanding of concepts and resources. Metacognitive: asks them to talk about how they understand the task and how to move forward together. Behavioral: draws attention to those who may not have participated. Socioemotional: appears when the tone heats up and asks for a friendlier conversation. Shared perspective: reminds them that the goal belongs to the group and asks for a common plan. Behavioral and shared perspective trigger only once, so they do not turn into nagging.
modos.como_age: This is the mode with the most signals (18), including uneven participation among members and signs of negative emotion [to be confirmed: the meaning of the signals]. It triggers the behavioral and shared perspective moves only once [to be confirmed whether the limit is per session or per group]. [to be confirmed]
